unitTitle: Multitenant Database Administration: CDB and PDB
title: Oracle Multitenant Quiz

questions.question: What is the primary structural role of the root container database (CDB$ROOT) in an Oracle Multitenant architecture?

answerOptions.text: It stores dedicated application schemas and tablespaces for individual IFS tenant environments.
answerOptions.rationale: User-created application schemas and tablespaces reside within individual User PDBs rather than the root container.

answerOptions.text: It functions as a system-supplied template used to provision new pluggable databases.
answerOptions.rationale: The system-supplied template for provisioning new containers is PDB$SEED, not CDB$ROOT.

answerOptions.text: It stores Oracle system metadata, common user accounts, and global initialization parameters.
answerOptions.rationale: The root container centrally manages Oracle system metadata, common users, and global memory/background processes for the entire CDB.

answerOptions.text: It enforces connection pool parameters exclusively for mid-tier application sessions.
answerOptions.rationale: Mid-tier application connection pools interact directly with dedicated PDB services rather than managing root settings.

questions.hint: Consider where global database initialization parameters and common user accounts reside versus application-specific data.

questions.question: In an Oracle Multitenant environment supporting IFS Applications, what is the specific role of PDB$SEED?

answerOptions.text: It contains active production ERP transaction data and user schemas.
answerOptions.rationale: Active production schemas and business transaction data reside within dedicated User PDBs.

answerOptions.text: It serves as a system-supplied template PDB used to rapidly provision new pluggable databases.
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Multitenant includes PDB$SEED specifically as a template for rapidly creating additional PDB instances.

answerOptions.text: It manages global background processes and shared SGA allocations across host memory.
answerOptions.rationale: Global background processes and shared memory structures are managed by CDB$ROOT.

answerOptions.text: It stores mid-tier connection configurations to prevent session leakage between environments.
answerOptions.rationale: Mid-tier context switching and connection isolation are managed by service routing and PDB isolation, not PDB$SEED.

questions.hint: Think about how new PDBs are rapidly provisioned when adding environments to a multitenant structure.

questions.question: Which sys_context call retrieves the name of the current container for an active database session?

answerOptions.text: sys_context('USERENV', 'CON_NAME')
answerOptions.rationale: The USERENV namespace parameter CON_NAME returns the exact name of the container context associated with the active session.

answerOptions.text: sys_context('DATABASE', 'PDB_NAME')
answerOptions.rationale: The namespace DATABASE is invalid for container identification in Oracle environment context calls.

answerOptions.text: sys_context('SESSION', 'CONTAINER_ID')
answerOptions.rationale: Retrieving container attributes requires querying the standard USERENV namespace with parameters such as CON_NAME or CON_ID.

answerOptions.text: sys_context('USERENV', 'DB_NAME')
answerOptions.rationale: The parameter DB_NAME returns the global database name rather than the specific container name in context.

questions.hint: Focus on the USERENV namespace attributes used to identify container names.

questions.question: Which pair of memory parameters can be configured per PDB to prevent runaway queries from exhausting host memory?

answerOptions.text: open_mode and container_id
answerOptions.rationale: These attributes represent operational state and container identification numbers in dynamic views, not configurable memory limits.

answerOptions.text: sga_target and pga_aggregate_limit
answerOptions.rationale: Setting sga_target and pga_aggregate_limit on a PDB establishes explicit memory boundaries to protect host resources from non-production workloads.

answerOptions.text: common_user_prefix and global_names
answerOptions.rationale: These settings relate to naming conventions and global database identification, not memory resource management.

answerOptions.text: db_create_file_dest and log_archive_dest
answerOptions.rationale: These parameters govern file system storage locations and redo log archiving destinations rather than memory caps.

questions.hint: Think about SGA and PGA allocation settings used to restrict memory per container.

questions.question: Which dynamic performance view is queried to inspect container IDs, names, and open modes for pluggable databases?

answerOptions.text: v$session
answerOptions.rationale: While v$session tracks active user sessions and session container IDs, it does not list pluggable database structures and open modes.

answerOptions.text: v$pdbs
answerOptions.rationale: The v$pdbs view provides container IDs, PDB names, and their operational open modes.

answerOptions.text: v$instance
answerOptions.rationale: The v$instance view provides status and operational state for the database instance as a whole rather than individual PDBs.

answerOptions.text: v$containers
answerOptions.rationale: The source material specifically demonstrates checking pluggable database states using v$pdbs.

questions.hint: Recall the dynamic performance view specifically named after pluggable databases.

questions.question: Which SQL command successfully switches an administrative session's context from CDB$ROOT to a pluggable database named ifsprod?

answerOptions.text: ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE ifsprod OPEN;
answerOptions.rationale: This command modifies the operational state of the PDB to open it for connections, but it does not alter the active session container context.

answerOptions.text: ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = ifsprod;
answerOptions.rationale: Executing ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER switches the current session context to the targeted PDB.

answerOptions.text: CONNECT / AS SYSDBA CONTAINER = ifsprod;
answerOptions.rationale: The CONNECT command syntax does not accept a CONTAINER keyword clause in this manner; context switching occurs via ALTER SESSION.

answerOptions.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET CONTAINER = ifsprod;
answerOptions.rationale: The ALTER SYSTEM statement modifies system-wide initialization parameters rather than session-level container contexts.

questions.hint: Look for the ALTER statement used to adjust session-level environment settings.

questions.question: In an Oracle Multitenant database, where are user-created tables, indexes, and application-specific metadata stored?

answerOptions.text: In the central CDB$ROOT system catalog.
answerOptions.rationale: CDB$ROOT manages system metadata and common objects across the container database, not individual application user schemas.

answerOptions.text: In the PDB$SEED template dictionary.
answerOptions.rationale: PDB$SEED is a read-only template database used exclusively for provisioning new PDBs.

answerOptions.text: In the private data dictionary of each dedicated User PDB.
answerOptions.rationale: Each User PDB maintains its own private data dictionary to isolate application schemas, tables, and indexes from other tenants.

answerOptions.text: In global SGA shared memory structures accessible by all containers.
answerOptions.rationale: Data dictionary definitions are stored within container-specific tablespaces on disk, not merely in volatile shared memory.

questions.hint: Recall where independent schema objects and user tables reside versus common system metadata.

questions.question: How can database administrators control CPU shares, parallel execution queues, and session limits for specific PDBs?

answerOptions.text: By assigning PDB Resource Manager Profiles.
answerOptions.rationale: PDB Resource Manager Profiles allow administrators to enforce specific allocations of CPU, parallel execution queues, and session thresholds per container.

answerOptions.text: By setting open_mode to read-only across all non-production instances.
answerOptions.rationale: Changing open modes restricts write access but does not regulate CPU allocation or parallel execution queues for active sessions.

answerOptions.text: By creating unique PDB$SEED templates for every environment.
answerOptions.rationale: Templates facilitate rapid provisioning but do not manage runtime CPU or session execution limits.

answerOptions.text: By consolidating all transactional schemas into CDB$ROOT.
answerOptions.rationale: Consolidating schemas into CDB$ROOT breaks multitenant isolation and does not provide per-PDB resource controls.

questions.hint: Consider the profiles used to restrict CPU, parallel queues, and session limits per container.

questions.question: What lifecycle advantage does pluggable database isolation offer when performing maintenance on individual IFS environments?

answerOptions.text: DBAs can unplug, clone, or drop an individual PDB without interrupting operations on sibling PDBs.
answerOptions.rationale: Logical and operational isolation allows independent maintenance tasks on one PDB without impacting sibling PDBs on the same container database.

answerOptions.text: Updating one PDB automatically updates the database kernel across all host servers.
answerOptions.rationale: PDB operations isolate schema and lifecycle tasks; they do not automatically modify underlying host kernels.

answerOptions.text: PDB isolation requires all non-production environments to be shut down whenever Release Updates are applied to CDB$ROOT.
answerOptions.rationale: Multitenant architecture simplifies patch alignment while preserving independent lifecycle management per PDB.

answerOptions.text: Dropping a PDB deletes common user accounts centrally maintained in CDB$ROOT.
answerOptions.rationale: Common user accounts are stored in CDB$ROOT and remain intact even if individual User PDBs are dropped.

questions.hint: Think about how tenant isolation affects maintenance tasks on sibling containers.

questions.question: Why is resource management critical across PDBs in a shared physical hardware environment supporting IFS Applications?

answerOptions.text: To prevent non-production workloads from degrading critical OLTP Production performance.
answerOptions.rationale: Resource management caps memory, CPU, and process usage on non-production containers to safeguard production ERP transactions from resource starvation.

answerOptions.text: To force all test scripts to execute directly inside CDB$ROOT.
answerOptions.rationale: Test scripts and non-production instances must run in isolated PDBs to avoid contaminating central system metadata or production data.

answerOptions.text: To ensure that all PDBs consume identical memory limits regardless of workload size.
answerOptions.rationale: Resource management allows precise, custom allocation of memory and CPU shares per container rather than uniform caps.

answerOptions.text: To automate the synchronization of Release Updates between DEV and PROD data dictionaries.
answerOptions.rationale: Resource management governs host resource consumption (CPU, SGA/PGA), not release update dictionary synchronization.

questions.hint: Focus on the primary operational goal of separating non-production workloads from production OLTP environments.
